title: Regina Jonas
hookLine: the first woman ordained a rabbi, in 1935, murdered at Auschwitz

lines: CAN A WOMAN BE A RABBI?
cards: A student in Berlin sits down to write a thesis. She is studying at a college that trains rabbis, and her question is one the people around her argue about: can a woman hold the office of rabbi?
She answers not with a feeling but with sources: the Bible, the Talmud, the codes of Jewish law, page after page. Her conclusion is yes. Her name is Regina Jonas.
The college lets her finish her studies, and then will not ordain her. So what does she do with a yes that nobody will sign?

teach.b: She keeps going. In 1935, a rabbi named Max Dienemann examined her privately and signed her rabbinic ordination. She is remembered as the first woman known to have been ordained a rabbi.
Germany was already under the Nazis, and Jewish life was being squeezed, rule by rule.

teach.h: A RABBI WHERE RABBIS HAD FLED.
teach.b: Congregations were losing their rabbis, who fled or were pushed out, and Regina Jonas went where she was needed: she preached, taught, visited the sick and the old, and comforted people who were losing everything.

Then she was deported to Theresienstadt, the ghetto and camp in the occupied Czech lands. Even there she kept working as a rabbi. She lectured, and helped meet the frightened people coming off the trains.
From there she was sent to Auschwitz, and murdered.
And then she was forgotten. For a long time her papers lay in an archive in Berlin, and her name dropped out of the story.
When they were found, the women who had become rabbis since learned that someone had gone before them.
In her own writing she argued, in effect, that God gives gifts and a calling to the heart without asking whether it belongs to a man or a woman.
So today's line is two words: the first. Not a trophy, but a weight. Being first meant arguing alone, serving in the worst of times, and then being lost.
Remembering her is part of the work.

how: Women rabbis and Jewish communities remember Regina Jonas in study, sermons and memorial events, and her papers are read today as part of the history of women in Jewish leadership.

games.q: you're Regina Jonas. you've finished your studies and written a thesis arguing a woman can be a rabbi. the college refuses to ordain you. what do you do?
o: give up, and teach children quietly instead.
keep going, and find a rabbi willing to examine and ordain you.
games.why: she kept going. a rabbi named Max Dienemann examined her privately and signed her ordination, and she served where she was needed until the camps.

practice: Who in your life did a thing before anyone like them had: the first in your family to finish school, the first woman in a job, the first to say something true out loud?
Think of what it cost them to go first, and what it made easier for whoever came after. If you pray, you can remember Regina Jonas in your own words; if not, simply say her name once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Regina Jonas. The Berlin woman ordained a rabbi in 1935, who served her people through the Nazi years and in Theresienstadt, and was murdered at Auschwitz. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the first. Her name was lost for years, and now it's found. Until tomorrow.
